transcript.text: Roomba i7 keeps stopping and saying Error 2. App says something about the brushes. We have a long haired dog.

I can't confirm exactly what 'Error 2' means on your i7 from the information I have, so I won't guess. But the app pointing at the brushes, plus a long-haired dog, makes the likely cause fairly clear. Robot vacuums stop themselves when the rollers can't turn freely, and long hair is the classic culprit. It rarely wraps round the middle of the rollers. It winds tightly into the ends: under the end caps and round the little axle pins, where you can't see it without pulling them out. Most likely causes, in order:
1. Hair wrapped round the roller ends, end caps or axle pins.
2. Hair or debris packed into the cleaning head housing, or tangled round the side brush.
3. Less likely: worn or damaged rollers, or a fault in the brush drive itself. Checks (lift it off the dock and switch it off first):
1. Turn it over on a towel. Release the yellow-tabbed roller guard/frame and lift out both rubber rollers.
2. Pull the end caps off each roller. They usually pull off by hand. Remove every bit of hair from the caps, the pins and the roller ends. Scissors or a seam ripper help with tight wraps. If you find a solid wad of hair here, that's probably your problem.
3. Look into the empty housing where the rollers sit, and clear any hair or grit, especially at the drive ends.
4. Check the side brush (the little spinning brush at the corner). Unscrew or pull it off if needed, clear any hair from under it, and check it spins freely.
5. Refit the rollers and turn each one by hand. They should spin smoothly with no grinding or catching. What the results mean: if it then runs without stopping, it was just hair, and with a long-haired dog a quick clean of the roller ends every week or two will stop it coming back. If the rollers look split, chewed or badly worn, they're a cheap and easy thing to renew. If everything is spotless and turns freely but it still stops with the brush error, the fault is more likely in the cleaning head drive. That's when it's worth contacting iRobot support or a repairer before buying anything. Let me know how you get on after clearing the rollers.

Right, did all that. Pulled the rubber brushes and the end caps off and there was thick hair wound round the axle under the yellow end caps. Cleaned the caps and bearings and refitted. Also found a hair tie stuck in the brush frame and removed it. Ran it on the kitchen floor and it was fine, then tried the thick rug and no error now.

That sounds sorted. Thick hair round the axles under the end caps, plus a hair tie in the frame, would easily drag the rollers enough to trigger the brush error. 1. Pull the end caps off and clear the axles every week or two. It only takes a minute, and it's far easier while the hair is a loose wisp than once it's packed tight.
2. Keep an eye on the side brush too, as hair builds up under it.
3. Empty the bin and tap out the filter regularly. Dog hair clogs it quickly and costs suction. If the rollers start to look split or worn down, or the brush error comes back even with everything clean, new rollers are cheap and easy to fit. If it still errors after that, contact iRobot support. Is there anything else I can help with?

candidates: Dog hair wrapped around the rubber roller ends, end caps or axle pins, stopping them turning freely (high)
Debris or hair packed into the cleaning head housing where the rollers sit, or round the side brush (medium)
Worn or damaged rollers, or a fault in the cleaning head drive (low)

plan: Already given by the customer, never ask for it again: make Roomba; model I7; code ERROR 2.
The fault they reported is: "keeps stopping". Keep to it: never describe a symptom, result or state they have not told you.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.

Explain what the error code means using ERROR CODES. If ERROR CODES does not resolve it, say plainly that you cannot confirm what it means on their model (it may not be an error code at all, for example part of the model name), never guess a meaning, and work from the symptoms.
